They are a currency unit. But, to generate it (mine it) you need to solve a mathematical equation. The first person to solve it gets the coins. The video cards are for mining.

Bitcoin GPU mining, aka transaction processing, has been over for about 3-4 years. It moved to ASIC chips ages ago.

Its all the other cryptocurrenies that are using them (ethereum, dash, monero, etc).

Blockchain tech is a public decentralized ledger that no one actor can control, its about as far from central banking as you can get and has the central banks pissing themselves in fear.

Every transaction is placed into a block; that block is than encrypted(The complexity of the encryption is based on the number of Nodes.(GPU's) looking for the key). All the millions of GPU's start looking for the key to that encryption. The first one to get the key correctly (or multiple in which they split the reward) receives 25 bitcoin. This is the incentive that creates stability for the systems infrastructure..

Bitcoins are a certain unique number that can only be discovered when you stumble on it. It is a bit like searching for prime numbers. You need brute force to try every single number and see if it is a prime number. In the beginning finding prime numbers (like bitcoins) are you need to test bigger and bigger numbers it gets harder and harder. So you need very fast CPU's in this case GPU's that are in video cards.

The more video cards you have the faster you can calculate and the faster you find new bigger prime numbers (bitcons).

When you buy or sell a bitcoin then you basically sell or buy a big number. But this big number has a purchase history that guarantees that you have the real number an not a stolen copy.

House Passes Medical Malpractice Tort Reform Bill

Gonna need a quick rundown on this and see if anybody has any thoughts, but I think this is kind of horrible. Maybe jaw-droppingly horrible.

Ostensibly, tort reform is sold by politicians as something that makes a crowded court system less crowded and makes insurance cost from frivolous lawsuits less expensive. On the surface tort reform sounds kind of good.

But I see it more as of a total corporate giveaway: more corporatism than free market. Since damages could now be limited, a lawsuit is now not as big of a deal to a big hospital or healthcare system. So the incentives towards careful patient care that minimizes mistakes and encourages hiring the best doctors (say born and primarily educated in US rather than in some 3rd world shithole) are greatly lessened.

And in the rare case that a doctor makes an egregious mistake (you go in to remove the right testicle and the doctor cuts out the left one, doctor fucks up some surgery egregiously and leaves you paralyzed, forgets to wash hands before surgery and infects you and you have to amputate arm, accidentally leaves a scalpel inside you, whatever) and your pain and suffering costs are capped. Is a quarter million sufficient for the worst medical errors?

Everybody has seen frivolous lawsuits, so tort reform is kind of an easy sell to the public, but in a worst case type of scenario, it feels like the actual victims get screwed to me.
